items.item: The hook's point only lands if the learner already half-recognizes one side of the translation (AWS); a learner with no cloud background at all gets a vocabulary list, not an 'aha' — the hook is written for the former audience deliberately

at.step: A job posting that looks unrelated to everything you know

items.item: The lock-in claim is structural (open format vs. non-exportable policy state), not a popularity or vendor-bias claim — a learner who reads it as 'AWS is better' has misread the argument

at.step: Which layer actually carries the switching cost?

items.item: Object storage and identity are genuinely swappable at the API-compatibility level for many workloads (S3-compatible APIs exist on other vendors), which is a stronger claim than 'the concept is similar' — it is why they're grouped with compute rather than with catalog/identity's policy problem

at.step: Object storage and identity, three names for the same job

items.item: A vendor renaming a product (Dataplex Universal Catalog → Knowledge Catalog, and GCP's own orchestration service's current name) does not change the underlying mechanism or this topic's table structure — the row survives the rename because the row names a job, not a product

at.step: Catalog and governance: the layer that just renamed itself

items.item: Fabric's bundling of three rows (storage, governance, compute) into one SaaS product is a packaging decision, not evidence that the three jobs have merged into one mechanism — OneLake, OneLake Catalog and Fabric Spark remain three separate services under one subscription

Synapse dedicated pools being 'maintained but not where new investment goes' is a roadmap signal worth teaching alongside the name, not a detail to drop — a learner planning a multi-year architecture needs to know which product in a cell is the one actually being invested in

This topic deliberately does not reproduce any mechanism locally (per CHAPTER.md's own scope); an expert reviewer should not expect or demand a code example here the way other full topics in this chapter provide one

The table's seven rows are not independent facts to memorize separately; grouping them by swap difficulty (compute/storage/identity vs. catalog/identity-policy) is the actual teaching content, and a learner who can recite all 21 product names but not which group each belongs to has not learned the topic's point

at.step: In one breath

items.item: Unity Catalog being cross-cloud (one product spanning AWS- and Azure-hosted Databricks) is the one exception to the per-vendor table structure, and it is worth calling out as an exception rather than silently fitting it into a single vendor's column

at.step: Catalog and governance: the layer that just renamed itself

items.item: Every product name quoted here is current as of this chapter's own research date; a reader encountering this topic even a year later should expect at least one more rename, which is the chapter's own disclosed experience writing it
